subject: Psychiatry
vignette: A 30-year-old man with schizophrenia is started on risperidone. His physician reviews how antipsychotics work, noting that both typical and atypical agents block dopamine D2 receptors, whereas atypical agents additionally block serotonin 5-HT2 receptors.
question: Which of the following best describes a distinguishing feature of atypical antipsychotics compared with typical antipsychotics?

options.text: They act exclusively as D2 partial agonists
They are dopamine D2 receptor agonists
They primarily treat only the positive symptoms of schizophrenia
They also block serotonin 5-HT2 receptors and treat both positive and negative symptoms
They have no dopamine receptor activity

explanation_correct: Atypical (second-generation) antipsychotics block dopamine D2 receptors and also block serotonin 5-HT2 receptors; they treat both positive and negative symptoms of schizophrenia. Typical (first-generation) agents primarily treat positive symptoms. Aripiprazole is a D2 partial agonist, but that is an exception among atypicals rather than a shared feature. Atypicals are antagonists at D2 (not agonists) and clearly retain dopamine receptor activity.

explanation_incorrect.A: Only aripiprazole is a D2 partial agonist among the atypicals; most atypical antipsychotics are D2 antagonists.
explanation_incorrect.B: Antipsychotics are dopamine receptor antagonists, not agonists; agonism at D2 would worsen psychosis.
explanation_incorrect.C: Treating primarily positive symptoms is characteristic of typical first-generation antipsychotics, not atypical agents.
explanation_incorrect.E: Atypical antipsychotics retain D2 receptor blockade; their defining addition is 5-HT2 blockade, not loss of dopaminergic activity.

educationalObjective: Atypical antipsychotics block both D2 and 5-HT2 receptors and treat positive and negative symptoms; aripiprazole is a D2 partial agonist.

subject: Psychiatry
vignette: A 27-year-old patient with schizophrenia is being started on an antipsychotic. The physician is choosing between haloperidol and olanzapine and reviewing to which generation each drug belongs.
question: Which of the following pairs correctly matches a drug with its antipsychotic class?
explanation_correct: Haloperidol is a high-potency typical (first-generation) antipsychotic, whereas olanzapine is an atypical (second-generation) agent. Clozapine, risperidone, quetiapine, aripiprazole, and olanzapine are atypical antipsychotics. Chlorpromazine and thioridazine are low-potency typical antipsychotics. Aripiprazole is an atypical D2 partial agonist.

explanation_incorrect.B: The classes are reversed: haloperidol is a typical antipsychotic and olanzapine is an atypical one.
explanation_incorrect.C: Both clozapine and risperidone are atypical second-generation antipsychotics, not typical agents.
explanation_incorrect.D: Chlorpromazine is a low-potency typical antipsychotic and quetiapine is an atypical antipsychotic, the reverse of this pairing.
explanation_incorrect.E: Aripiprazole is an atypical partial agonist and thioridazine is a low-potency typical antipsychotic, the reverse of this pairing.

educationalObjective: Haloperidol, chlorpromazine, and thioridazine are typical antipsychotics; clozapine, olanzapine, risperidone, quetiapine, and aripiprazole are atypical.

subject: Psychiatry
vignette: A 33-year-old man with schizophrenia has been treated with adequate trials of haloperidol and risperidone, yet has persistent auditory hallucinations and multiple psychiatric hospitalizations. He has also made two suicide attempts. His physician is considering a medication reserved for psychotic disorders that have failed other agents and for persistent suicidality.
question: Which of the following is the most appropriate antipsychotic for this patient?
explanation_correct: Clozapine is used for treatment-resistant psychotic disorders and for patients with persistent suicidality (cloze to the edge). This patient has failed multiple adequate antipsychotic trials and continues to have suicidal behavior. Haloperidol, fluphenazine, pimozide, and thioridazine are first-generation agents and are not the reserved option for treatment resistance. Clozapine requires close WBC monitoring for agranulocytosis.

explanation_incorrect.A: Haloperidol is a high-potency typical antipsychotic that he has already failed in an adequate trial.
explanation_incorrect.B: Fluphenazine is a high-potency typical antipsychotic and is not the agent reserved for treatment-resistant psychosis with suicidality.
explanation_incorrect.C: Pimozide is a high-potency typical antipsychotic, also used in Tourette syndrome, and is not indicated for refractory schizophrenia with suicidality.
explanation_incorrect.D: Thioridazine is a low-potency typical antipsychotic with prominent antimuscarinic effects and retinal deposits, not a treatment-resistance option.

educationalObjective: Clozapine is reserved for treatment-resistant psychotic disorders and persistent suicidality, with WBC monitoring required.

subject: Psychiatry
vignette: A 45-year-old woman with schizophrenia is started on chlorpromazine. She soon reports profound drowsiness, dry mouth, constipation, and lightheadedness on standing. Her physician recognizes these as the anti-HAM effects of low-potency typical antipsychotics.
question: Which of the following best explains this patient's symptoms?

options.text: Antihistaminic sedation, anti-alpha-1 orthostatic hypotension, and antimuscarinic dry mouth and constipation
Dopamine D2 blockade in the tuberoinfundibular pathway
Increased dopaminergic activity in the nigrostriatal pathway

explanation_correct: Low-potency typical antipsychotics such as chlorpromazine and thioridazine have prominent antihistaminic (sedation), anti-alpha-1-adrenergic (orthostatic hypotension), and antimuscarinic (dry mouth, constipation) effects, summarized as anti-HAM. D2 blockade in the tuberoinfundibular pathway instead causes hyperprolactinemia. Atypical agents block, not stimulate, 5-HT2 receptors. Nigrostriatal D2 blockade, not increased activity, causes extrapyramidal symptoms. Seizures are a dose-related clozapine effect.

explanation_incorrect.B: Tuberoinfundibular D2 blockade produces hyperprolactinemia with galactorrhea and oligomenorrhea, not sedation and antimuscarinic effects.
explanation_incorrect.C: Atypical antipsychotics block serotonin 5-HT2 receptors; 5-HT2 stimulation does not explain these antimuscarinic and antihistaminic effects.
explanation_incorrect.D: Antipsychotics reduce nigrostriatal dopaminergic activity; increased activity would not produce the anti-HAM effects described.
explanation_incorrect.E: Dose-related seizures are a clozapine adverse effect, not the cause of drowsiness and constipation from chlorpromazine.

educationalObjective: Low-potency typicals cause anti-HAM effects: antihistaminic sedation, anti-alpha-1 orthostasis, and antimuscarinic dry mouth and constipation.

subject: Psychiatry
vignette: A 26-year-old man with treatment-resistant schizophrenia is started on clozapine. After several months he has gained 12 kg, and laboratory studies show hyperglycemia and hypertriglyceridemia. His physician counsels him about metabolic monitoring.
question: Which of the following adverse effects is most strongly associated with clozapine and olanzapine?
explanation_correct: Metabolic effects, including weight gain, hyperglycemia, and dyslipidemia, are increased with clozapine and olanzapine (obesity) and warrant metabolic monitoring. Corneal deposits are caused by chlorpromazine and retinal deposits by thioridazine. Acute dystonia is an early extrapyramidal effect of high-potency typicals. Agranulocytosis and dose-related seizures are specific clozapine toxicities, but the findings in this patient are the metabolic effects. QT prolongation is a cardiac effect seen with several antipsychotics.

explanation_incorrect.A: Corneal deposits are an ophthalmologic adverse effect of chlorpromazine, not a metabolic effect of clozapine or olanzapine.
explanation_incorrect.C: Acute dystonia occurs hours to days after starting high-potency typical antipsychotics and presents with muscle spasm and oculogyric crisis.
explanation_incorrect.D: Agranulocytosis and seizures are serious clozapine toxicities, but they do not explain this patient's weight gain and hyperglycemia.
explanation_incorrect.E: QT prolongation is a cardiac adverse effect; it is not the metabolic disturbance described in this patient.

educationalObjective: Clozapine and olanzapine carry the highest risk of metabolic effects: weight gain, hyperglycemia, and dyslipidemia.

subject: Psychiatry
vignette: A 29-year-old woman with schizophrenia started taking clozapine 3 months ago and has been receiving scheduled blood tests. She now presents with fever and a sore throat. Laboratory studies reveal a white blood cell count of 900/mm3 with severe neutropenia.
question: Which of the following adverse effects necessitated the monitoring that should have detected this complication?
explanation_correct: Clozapine causes agranulocytosis, requiring close monitoring of WBC counts (monitor WBCs clozely). Fever and sore throat with severe neutropenia are the classic presentation. Clozapine also causes dose-related seizures, myocarditis, and hypersalivation, but these are not detected by WBC monitoring. Hyperprolactinemia results from reduced tuberoinfundibular dopaminergic activity and is more typical of high-potency D2 blockers.

explanation_incorrect.A: Dose-related seizures are a clozapine risk but are not screened for with white blood cell counts.
explanation_incorrect.B: Myocarditis is a clozapine adverse effect that presents with cardiac findings, not neutropenia on a blood count.
explanation_incorrect.C: Hypersalivation is a bothersome clozapine effect but is not life threatening and is not monitored with WBC counts.
explanation_incorrect.E: Hyperprolactinemia causes galactorrhea, oligomenorrhea, and gynecomastia through tuberoinfundibular D2 blockade and is not detected by WBC monitoring.

educationalObjective: Clozapine requires close WBC monitoring because of agranulocytosis; its other effects include seizures, myocarditis, and hypersalivation.

subject: Psychiatry
vignette: A 30-year-old patient with schizophrenia has prominent auditory hallucinations and delusions but also flat affect, social withdrawal, and lack of motivation. The physician is choosing between a first-generation and a second-generation antipsychotic.
question: Which of the following best explains why a second-generation (atypical) antipsychotic may be preferred in this patient?

options.text: Atypical agents treat both positive and negative symptoms, whereas typical agents primarily treat positive symptoms
Atypical antipsychotics are the only agents that treat positive symptoms
Typical antipsychotics are more effective for negative symptoms
Atypical antipsychotics have no dopaminergic activity
Typical antipsychotics primarily treat negative symptoms

explanation_correct: Typical (first-generation) antipsychotics primarily treat the positive symptoms of schizophrenia, such as hallucinations and delusions, whereas atypical (second-generation) agents treat both positive and negative symptoms, including flat affect and social withdrawal. This patient has both symptom domains, favoring an atypical agent. Atypical drugs still block D2 receptors, so they retain dopaminergic activity. Clozapine specifically is reserved for treatment resistance.

explanation_incorrect.B: Typical antipsychotics also treat positive symptoms; the advantage of atypicals is added efficacy against negative symptoms.
explanation_incorrect.C: Typical antipsychotics are less effective for negative symptoms, which is why an atypical agent is favored here.
explanation_incorrect.D: Atypical antipsychotics block dopamine D2 receptors and therefore do have dopaminergic activity.
explanation_incorrect.E: Typical antipsychotics primarily treat positive, not negative, symptoms.

educationalObjective: Atypical antipsychotics treat both positive and negative symptoms of schizophrenia; typicals mainly treat positive symptoms.

subject: Psychiatry
vignette: Two patients with schizophrenia are started on different first-generation antipsychotics. Patient 1 receives haloperidol and soon develops muscle stiffness and tremor. Patient 2 receives thioridazine and complains of sedation, dry mouth, and orthostatic hypotension with few neurologic symptoms.
question: Which of the following best explains the difference in adverse effect profiles between these two drugs?

options.text: Haloperidol is low potency with greater antimuscarinic effects; thioridazine is high potency with greater neurologic effects
Both drugs are atypical antipsychotics with identical receptor-binding profiles
Haloperidol is high potency with greater D2 affinity and neurologic effects; thioridazine is low potency with more antihistaminic, anti-alpha-1, and antimuscarinic effects
Thioridazine is an atypical agent associated with metabolic syndrome
Haloperidol causes retinal deposits, whereas thioridazine causes corneal deposits

explanation_correct: High-potency typical antipsychotics (haloperidol, trifluoperazine, pimozide, fluphenazine) have greater D2 receptor affinity and more neurologic adverse effects such as extrapyramidal symptoms and neuroleptic malignant syndrome. Low-potency typicals (chlorpromazine, thioridazine) produce more antihistaminic, anti-alpha-1-adrenergic, and antimuscarinic effects. Option E reverses the ophthalmologic effects: chlorpromazine causes corneal deposits and thioridazine causes retinal deposits. Both drugs are first-generation agents.

explanation_incorrect.A: The potency and adverse effect profiles are reversed: haloperidol is high potency with more neurologic effects, and thioridazine is low potency with more antimuscarinic effects.
explanation_incorrect.B: Haloperidol and thioridazine are both first-generation (typical) antipsychotics and differ markedly in potency and receptor effects.
explanation_incorrect.D: Thioridazine is a low-potency typical antipsychotic, not an atypical agent, and metabolic syndrome is associated mainly with clozapine and olanzapine.
explanation_incorrect.E: The ophthalmologic effects are reversed: chlorpromazine causes corneal deposits and thioridazine causes retinal deposits.

educationalObjective: High-potency typicals cause more EPS and NMS; low-potency typicals cause more anti-HAM effects. Chlorpromazine deposits in the cornea, thioridazine in the retina.
